title: Internal Spearphishing via Trusted Accounts
summary: This detection strategy covers T1534, Internal Spearphishing, where an adversary who already controls one mailbox or chat account sends convincing messages to colleagues inside the same organisation, often to harvest credentials or move the intrusion to a better placed user. It matters because trust comes from the sender address, so recipients and gateway filters treat the message as internal mail and defences that block external phishing are bypassed. The telemetry that makes it visible is mail and collaboration metadata: message trace records with sender, recipient count, subject shape, and link destination, unified audit records for mailbox rule and permission changes, and identity sign-in records for the sending account. The main failure is sensitivity: colleagues send each other links and attachments all day, so the rule must anchor on a change in the sending account rather than on message content.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for phishing that comes from inside your own organisation. An attacker who takes over one account uses it to mail colleagues. The message looks internal, so people trust it more. This rule studies the sending account and the message spread instead of the message text.
beginner.whyItMatters: Filters usually trust mail from your own domain, so internal phishing slips past them. Colleagues reply and click because the sender is familiar. One stolen mailbox can therefore reach hundreds of people quickly. The signal is in the account behaviour, such as a sudden wide send or a new mail rule. That behaviour is easier to spot than the wording of each message.
howItWorks: The mail service records each message with the sender, recipients, and link details.
The identity service records each sign in with the client and the network location.
The rule measures how far the message spread and how the subject or link style differs from that sender history.
It checks whether the account changed mail rules, forwarding, or permissions in the same period.
It compares the sending session against the recent baseline for that account and device.
A wide send from a new location, with a new rule or forwarding change, raises the alert.
beginner.example: Think of a school where pupils only need a note from a teacher to leave early. A stranger cannot write one, but a pupil who steals a teacher stamp can sign many notes. Other teachers see the stamp and let pupils go without a second look. Internal phishing works the same way. The stamp is the internal sender address. The unusual number of notes is what gives it away.
takeaways: Internal messages inherit trust, so defenses that block external phishing often do not apply.
The strongest signal is a change in how an account sends or forwards mail, not the wording of one message.
A quick check of new mail rules and forwarding on a suspect account reveals most internal phishing setups.

objectives: Explain what internal spearphishing is and why internal mail bypasses common filters.
Identify the message trace, audit, and sign-in telemetry needed to detect it.
Describe how to use sender history to detect an abnormal message spread.
Write a pseudo rule that pairs a wide internal send with a new mail forwarding rule.
Explain how mailbox permission changes support internal phishing at scale.
Recommend containment steps that stop the campaign without blocking the whole domain.
dataSources: Microsoft 365 unified audit log records for mailbox rule creation, forwarding settings, and permission grants
Exchange Online message trace records with sender, recipient list, subject, and uniform resource locator details
Entra ID sign-in logs with client application, network location, and authentication method for the sending account
Mail security gateway logs showing internal to internal messages and their verdicts
Collaboration platform audit records for direct message sends and file share links created by the account
logic: The rule links a change in the sending account with a change in message behaviour. It joins unified audit records for mailbox rule creation, forwarding, or permission changes with message trace records that show a wide internal send from the same account inside a short window, and with sign-in records for the session that made both changes. The malicious case is an account that creates a forwarding or hiding rule and then sends messages with a similar subject and link shape to many internal recipients from a new network location or an unfamiliar client. The benign case is an internal announcement from a communications team, a marketing campaign sent through an approved platform, or a colleague sharing a document after changing their own mail settings for personal convenience. The recipient count against the sender baseline, the rule change, and the sign-in location are the fields that separate them.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Internal Mail Burst With New Forwarding Rule From New Location
# logsource:
#   product: azure
# detection:
#   selection:
#     Operation|contains: New-InboxRule, Set-Mailbox, Add-MailboxPermission
#   burst:
#     Operation: Send
#     RecipientCount: greater_than_20
#     RecipientDomain: internal
#   condition: selection and burst
# level: high
falsePositives: Internal communications teams sending an approved all staff announcement through a shared mailbox
Automated business systems that mail a daily report or notification to a large internal distribution list
Employees who legitimately configure forwarding to a personal device before an approved leave period
Recruitment and human resources campaigns that send a personalised message to many internal recipients
tuningNotes: Baseline the normal recipient count, subject style, and sending client for each mailbox for sixty days, then exclude the approved bulk senders, shared mailboxes, and distribution list owners by name. Keep the high severity tier for individual user accounts whose send volume or rule configuration changes, and route known bulk senders to a review report instead of an alert. Filter out messages sent through the approved marketing and survey platforms, since those never travel from a user mailbox. This narrowing means a slow internal phishing effort of five messages a day will not alert, so monitor new forwarding and hiding rules on their own as a separate high severity rule.
